opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot. My view is that AI is not going to reduce the need for scientists. If anything, it's going to change what it means to be a scientist, and I think in a very exciting way.

What we're starting to see with these models is that they can do a lot of the work that used to take a very long time: going through the literature, checking calculations, trying out a bunch of different approaches to a problem, even proving some small lemmas. I've had experiences myself where I give a model a problem I've been thinking about, and it comes back with something genuinely useful, sometimes something I hadn't thought of. So the bottleneck shifts. It's less about grinding through the technical details and more about asking the right questions, having taste, knowing which problems actually matter, and being able to verify and make sense of what comes out.

For academia, I think this is a moment to really rethink things. Academia has always been the place where people pursue curiosity-driven research, the long-term, risky stuff that doesn't have an immediate payoff. That role becomes even more important now, because suddenly every researcher has access to something like a very capable collaborator, almost a team of postdocs. A single professor with a few students could potentially explore far more ideas than before. So the scale of what an individual or a small group can accomplish goes way up.

That said, there are real challenges. How do we train the next generation? If the model can do the exercises, how do students build the deep intuition you need to judge whether an answer is right? I think education will have to emphasize understanding and critical thinking even more, and learning to work with these tools rather than pretending they don't exist. And there are questions about credit, about how we evaluate research, and about how peer review works when so much can be generated quickly.

But overall I'm very optimistic. I really believe we're going to see an acceleration of science, and the people who embrace these tools, who stay curious and keep asking deep questions, are going to be able to do things that were just unimaginable a few years ago. The need for scientists isn't going away. It's the ambition of science that's going to grow.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will not reduce the need for scientists and that science’s ambition will grow, but it does not clearly argue that AI increases the need for scientists.

r002.rationale: It says researchers can explore far more ideas and that the scale of what an individual or small group can accomplish will rise.

r003.rationale: It identifies training the next generation and helping students build intuition, understanding, and critical thinking as challenges for academia.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's funny, because people sometimes expect me to say that AI is going to replace scientists, and I actually think it's almost the opposite. What's going to change is the *shape* of the job, not the need for it.

Let me explain what I mean. When I was doing pure mathematics, a huge fraction of my time was spent on what I'd call the mechanical part of research. You have an idea, and then you spend three weeks checking whether the inequality actually goes in the right direction, whether the constant is really bounded, whether somebody already proved this in 1987 in a paper you've never heard of. That part is going away. The models are already very good at it, and they're getting better every few months. So the ratio of time spent on taste, on deciding which question is worth asking, versus time spent on verification and grinding, that ratio is going to shift dramatically.

And I think that's where the role of the scientist actually becomes more important, not less. Because the hard part was never really the grinding. The hard part is knowing what matters. Knowing which of the ten thousand true theorems is the interesting one. Knowing which experiment, if it came out one way or the other, would actually change how we think. That's a kind of judgment that comes from being deeply embedded in a community, in a tradition of thought, and I don't see the models having that in the near term. They can have a lot of knowledge, but taste is something that is formed by caring about a problem for a long time.

Now, academia specifically. I'll be a little bit provocative here. I think academia has to rethink what it's for, because for a long time the implicit contract was: we train people for many years so they can produce technical results. If the technical results can increasingly be produced by a system, then the training has to be about something else. It has to be about asking questions. It has to be about judgment, about understanding why a result matters, about being able to critique what the AI gives you back. In a way, academia should become more like what it was always supposed to be, which is a place for thinking, and less like a factory for papers.

The other thing I'd say, and this is something I feel quite strongly about, is that the frontier of the science itself is moving. A lot of the most interesting scientific questions right now are about these systems. Why do they work? What is it that they're actually learning? What are the limits? These are deep questions, and they're questions where academia has a real advantage, because you can take the long view, you can study something for five years without needing it to ship. So I actually think there's an enormous opportunity for academia, if it's willing to engage with the technology seriously rather than at arm's length.

So, to summarize, more scientists, not fewer. But scientists who spend their time on the parts that were always the most human, which is deciding what's worth knowing.

r001.rationale: The response says the scientist’s role becomes more important and concludes, “more scientists, not fewer.”

r002.rationale: It says AI will take over much of the mechanical checking and grinding, freeing scientists to spend more time on judgment and choosing questions—communicating increased research productivity.

r003.rationale: It says academia should train people in asking questions, exercising judgment, understanding why results matter, and critiquing AI outputs.

astra-6.text:
I think advances in AI should make us more ambitious about science. If we can automate more of the work involved in answering a question, that doesn’t mean we’ve run out of work for scientists. It means we can ask questions that were previously out of reach.

But the role does change. There’s more emphasis on choosing the right problems, identifying which assumptions to challenge, and figuring out what would actually constitute convincing evidence. An AI producing a plausible explanation is not the same thing as understanding nature. You still need to test it.

And academia has a very important role here. We need places where people can pursue questions whose value isn’t obvious today, where they can challenge the direction everyone else is taking, and where the goal is to build knowledge that is shared. AI could give many more researchers the ability to explore ambitious ideas. I would like to see academia use that opportunity to take more intellectual risks.

r001.rationale: The response says AI lets scientists pursue questions previously out of reach and that this creates more work for scientists, supporting an increased need.

r002.rationale: It says AI can automate more of the work involved in answering questions, enabling scientists to tackle more ambitious ideas.

r003.rationale: It describes academia as supporting risky, open-ended research, but does not identify developing scientists’ expertise as a role.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes scientists more important, but it changes where we should put our effort. If AI can help us work through calculations, write code, or explore possible explanations, then the scarce resource becomes knowing what question to ask. What is worth understanding? What experiment would actually distinguish between two ideas? Those are scientific judgments.

And academia has a very important role there. You want places where people can pursue questions that might not have an immediate commercial payoff, where they can challenge the assumptions behind these systems, and where results can be examined openly. That becomes even more valuable as the technology becomes more powerful.

For education, I think the challenge is to let students use these tools while still developing their own judgment. Getting an answer is different from understanding why it’s right, where it might fail, and how you would check it. We should train people to do that. The opportunity is to give more people the ability to participate in science, and to let scientists be more ambitious about the problems they tackle.

r001.rationale: It says scientists become more important as AI advances.

r002.rationale: It describes AI helping scientists with calculations, code, and exploring explanations, communicating that AI can make their work more productive.

r003.rationale: It says education should help students use AI while developing their own judgment, and that people should be trained to assess and check AI-assisted answers.
